newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia set for 3 pct budget deficit -- minister.
newsitem.headline: Namibia set for 3 pct budget deficit -- minister.

text.p: Namibia was on course to achieve a budget deficit target of about three percent by the year 2000, but still suffered the burdern of a bloated public sector, Finance Minister Nangolo Mbumba said on Wednesday.
Delivering his budget speech for 1997/98, Mbumba said the government was determined to reduce expenditure levels.
"Given the available resources for the 1997/98 fiscal year, the budget has been formulated not to exceed a deficit level of 3.7 percent of the expected GDP," he told parliament.

The deficit level for the financial year ending March 31 would probably be closer to four percent than the estimated 4.9 percent, Mbumba said, adding that this indicated considerable deficiences in the planning and implementation capacities of various ministries.

Total estimated revenue for 1997/98 would be up by almost 15 percent to 5.99 billion Nambian dollars, mainly due to further growth in Namibia's revenue from the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), which groups South Africa, Lesotho, Swaziland, Botswana and Namibia.
"Revenue from the Customs Union in 1997/98 has become the largest single tax category," Mbumba said.
But Henning Melber, director of the Namibian Economic Policy Research Unit, warned that SACU income would drop.

"Under the World Trade discussions, and the present free trade negotiations between South Africa and the European Union, SACU income will decrease considerably in the near future. So for the government it poses the problem: where do they get compensation for the loss in income?"
Total expenditure proposed for 1997/98 will rise less steeply than last year to 5,755 billion Namibian dollars, an increase of 13.4 percent, compared to 17 percent in the previous financial year.
The shift is to more capital and development expenditure, which now forms 17.4 percent of the total budget.

Mbumba admitted that the bloated public sector remained one of the government's biggest headaches, but said recommendations of the Wage and Salaries Commission (WASCOM) for a leaner civil service had been implemented selectively.
For the coming financial year 2.6 billion Namibian dollars have been earmarked for personnel-related expenditure, a 14-percent rise in the wage bill compared to last year's budget.
Melber said this was still the budget's central problem.

"The civil service wage bill remains the achilles heel. The current expenditure amounts to more than 45 percent of the total budget and that is unsustainable. The number of funded posts in the public service has again increased by 3.5 percent," he said.
Given the slow progess in public sector reform, Mbumba announced that the second phase of salary adjustments recommended under WASCOM would be put on hold.

He touched on current commercialisation and eventual privatisation plans as a means of reducing the civil service wage bill: establishing NamWater Corporation was in the pipeline to commercialise bulk water supply, while commercialising airports would be investigated.

While there would be no immediate changes to the tax regime, Mbumba announced a general overhaul of the tax system which would include probing the feasibility of value added tax and its possible introduction after 1998.
The Namibian business community has been hoping for this to get rid of the current sales tax and additional sales duty.
As in previous years, the biggest slice of the cake goes to education, health and social services.
This is in line with the goals set out in the National Development Plan, the medium-term economic strategy that seeks to improve lives and alleviate poverty.

Only the defence budget held a minor surprise with a steeper than expected increase. "A somewhat irritating phenomenon is the 41-percent increase proposed for the ministry of defence," Melber commented.

Melber added, however, that the increase covered mainly personnel expenditure and not the acquisition of hardware and could therefore almost be regarded as social expenditure probably designed to finance employing former soldiers.
--- Johannesburg newsroom (27-11) 482-1003
